extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders and commenters (employers, employees, state/local governments, researchers, economists, industry groups)
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and Preliminary Economic Analysis (PEA) for OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard, including legal justification, alternatives analysis, industry/employee exposure profiling, data sources, and scope/exemption definitions for estimating affected entities and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative externalities in the labor market
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the costs of occupational injury and illness are borne by parties other than individual employers or employees; the major source of these negative externalities is the occupational injury or illness cost that workers' compensation does not cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because employers and employees often do not bear the full costs (health care, rehabilitation, retraining, direct income maintenance, life insurance paid by society), these externalized costs are ignored in labor market negotiations, potentially producing an inefficiently high level of occupational risk. (Printed page 70805)

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect competition undermining compensating differentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Labor markets are fragmented and characterized by search frictions and employer market power, so employers may not be wage-takers and can influence wages and employment conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search costs, limited information, firm-specific human capital, relocation costs, and compensation components that are not transferable (e.g., pensions, seniority) can allow employers to offer lower-than-competitive wages and less than full compensation for health and safety risks, reducing incentives to invest in workplace safety. (Printed page 70805–70806)

rubrics_metrics.name: Information dissemination alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary or mandatory information programs (akin to Hazard Communication) may improve information but would not by themselves provide adequate employee protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include employer incentives not to gather/distribute exposure data absent regulation, employees' limited ability to evaluate risk information, persistence of externalities and imperfect competition, and the fact that even efficient-market wage premiums may underprovide safety relative to social values. OSHA therefore incorporates hazard communication into a broader standard rather than relying solely on information dissemination. (Printed page 70806)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on workers' compensation payouts
rubrics_metrics.description: State workers' compensation systems impose limitations that prevent full shifting of injury and illness costs to employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated limitations include: caps on wage replacement based on state average wage rather than worker's actual wage; restrictions on which medical services are compensated and amounts; no compensation for non-pecuniary losses (pain and suffering); limited or no cost-of-living increases; restrictions on duration or absolute ceilings on disability benefits; and low absolute ceilings on death benefits. These constraints mean workers' compensation does not fully internalize costs. (Printed page 70806–70807)

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence between workers' compensation premiums and workplace risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers' compensation premium-setting mechanisms (class rating, experience rating, assigned risk pools) often fail to reflect an individual employer's actual workplace risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 85% of employers have class-rated premiums based on industry history; experience ratings (where used) are based on past payments not on overall safety program quality; risk spreading protects against catastrophic loss but reduces incentives because premium reductions for improved safety are muted, creating moral hazard. Insurers may refuse coverage, but assigned risk pools provide coverage at mandated rates. (Printed page 70807–70808)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tort liability is an inadequate alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: The tort system generally cannot substitute for regulation in shifting costs or protecting workers from heat-related injuries and illnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers' compensation 'exclusive remedy' provisions bar most suits against employers; proving gross negligence for transient, localized heat conditions is difficult; third-party defendants are unlikely to exist for heat exposures; tort suits are costly. Thus, tort liability is severely limited as an alternative mechanism. (Printed page 70807)

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA's statutory justification for proposing the standard
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's primary reasons for proposing the heat standard are based on the requirements of the OSH Act and findings that employees in many industries are exposed to environmental and process heat hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor market failures and insufficiency of alternatives (information programs, workers' compensation, tort) support the need for a regulatory standard to achieve a socially optimal level of protection. (Printed page 70807–70808)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'core industries' with highest heat exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA considers certain industries to be 'core industries' where employees have the most exposure to heat-related hazards (outdoors, radiant heat sources, or insufficient indoor temperature control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core industries listed explicitly: Agriculture, Forestry, and Fishing; Building Materials and Equipment Suppliers; Commercial Kitchens; Construction; Drycleaning and Commercial Laundries; Landscaping and Facilities Support; Maintenance and Repair; Manufacturing; Oil and Gas; Postal and Delivery Services; Recreation and Amusement; Sanitation and Waste Removal; Telecommunications; Temporary Help Services; Transportation; Utilities; and Warehousing. OSHA also states employees in other industries may be covered depending on job tasks (e.g., maintenance, landscaping). (Printed page 70808)

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary data source for economic profile: SUSB 2017
rubrics_metrics.description: Most economic data on number of firms, establishments, employment, and annual receipts are sourced from the Census Bureau's Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) 2017 dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SUSB presents data by NAICS code, employee class size, and State. OSHA uses SUSB definitions for establishments, firms, employment, and annual receipts but supplements SUSB where it omits sectors (e.g., agriculture, some government entities). (Printed page 70808–70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative data and methods for agricultural industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Because most agricultural industries are not included in SUSB, OSHA used the Department of Agriculture's 2017 Census of Agriculture to derive estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used counts of farms as establishments, assumed number of firms equals number of establishments, used 'workers' on hired labor farms as employment, and 'total sales' as annual receipts. OSHA solicits feedback on alternative sources and methods. (Printed page 70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative data and methods for local governments
rubrics_metrics.description: SUSB excludes most government entities, so OSHA used Census Government Units Survey (GUS) and Census of Governments data to estimate local government counts, employment, and receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumed each entity = one firm = one establishment, used GUS for counts, used Census of Governments Survey of Public Employment & Payroll for employment, and derived annual receipts per entity by estimating average receipts per resident and multiplying by entity population. OSHA requests comment on methods. (Printed page 70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative data and methods for State governments
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments excluded from SUSB; OSHA assumed each State government equals one firm and one establishment and used Census of Governments and Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances for employment and receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used 2022 Census of Governments employment data and 2021 Annual Survey revenue data to estimate State government impacts. Comments on assumptions welcomed. (Printed page 70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of QCEW to fill gaps for certain industries (Rail, Postal, Insurance/Benefit Funds)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Rail Transportation (NAICS 4821), Postal and Delivery Services (NAICS 4911), and Insurance and Employee Benefit Funds (NAICS 5251), OSHA derived estimates from the BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used QCEW establishment and employment counts by State, assumed each establishment = unique firm, and converted QCEW wages into annual receipts using the receipts-to-wages ratio from SUSB for each State. (Printed page 70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: one establishment equals one firm where data lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where data on firms is not available (e.g., governments, agriculture, postal services, rail transportation) OSHA assumed one establishment equals one firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explicitly notes this assumption and invites comment on alternative approaches. This assumption affects counts of affected entities for industries with missing firm-level data. (Printed page 70809)

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of States into NWS geographic regions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA grouped States into geographic regions based on National Weather Service (NWS) regions for the PEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table VIII.B.1 presents the mapping of States/territories into Alaskan, Central, Eastern, Pacific, Southern, and Western regions. Geographic variation matters because costs differ by location due to environmental conditions. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Climatic work conditions and O*NET frequency-to-days mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used O*NET data to define four climatic work conditions and mapped O*NET frequency categories to minimum/maximum days and estimated percentage of days (based on a 250-day work year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climatic categories: (1) Indoors, Environmentally Controlled; (2) Indoors, Not Environmentally Controlled; (3) Outdoors, Exposed to Weather; (4) Outdoors, Under Cover. O*NET frequency categories 'Never' through 'Every Day' were mapped to day ranges and estimated percentage of days (e.g., 'Every Day' = 250 days = 100%). Table VIII.B.2 shows the mapping used. OSHA assumes employees in conditions (2),(3),(4) are in-scope unless exempt. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating percent of employees in climatic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimated the percent of employees working regularly in each climatic condition by occupation using O*NET frequencies, mapped day percentages, and OEWS industry employment shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each SOC occupation, OSHA multiplied the percent in each O*NET frequency bracket by the estimated percentage of days for that bracket, then multiplied by the percent of industry employment in that occupation from OEWS (May 2022), and aggregated to 4-digit NAICS to estimate percent of industry employees in each climatic condition. For missing SOC codes, OSHA used averages from similar occupations. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor environmentally controlled exclusion (unless process heat exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees working indoors in environmentally controlled settings are considered out of scope unless they are exposed to process heat (e.g., kitchens, foundries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some process-heat exposures might be categorized in O*NET as 'Indoors, Environmentally Controlled,' OSHA also relied on ORS data to identify occupations exposed to process heat; combining methods may overstate counts if overlap exists. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ORS to identify exposure to process heat
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used the BLS Occupational Requirements Survey (ORS) to identify occupations exposed to extreme/process heat, multiplying the ORS exposure percentages by industry employment shares to estimate process-heat exposed employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ORS provides percent of employees exposed to extreme heat by SOC occupation; OSHA multiplied ORS percentages by OEWS industry occupation shares and added these to climatic-condition exposure percentages to get total percent exposed. OSHA notes ORS uses a higher temperature criterion than the proposed 80°F trigger, which may undercount some exposures. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledged temperature-threshold mismatch between ORS and proposed trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: ORS's definition of exposure to extreme heat has a higher temperature criterion than the proposed standard's initial heat trigger of 80°F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes this mismatch may lead to an undercount of employees exposed to process heat when relying solely on ORS for identification. (Printed page 70810)

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate method for estimating total potentially affected employees
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA computed total potentially affected employees by adding the percent exposed via climatic conditions to the percent exposed to process heat and multiplying by OEWS employment totals for each industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The percentage exposures (from O*NET and ORS methods) were combined and applied to OEWS May 2022 employment totals by industry to produce counts of potentially affected employees. (Printed page 70810–70811)

rubrics_metrics.name: Six scope exemptions defining employees not covered by the proposed standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers or employees exclusively performing work activities that meet one or more of six definitions are exempt from the proposed standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six exemptions are: (1) work activities with no reasonable expectation of exposure at or above the initial heat trigger; (2) work activities where the employee is exposed above the initial heat trigger for fifteen minutes or less in any sixty-minute period; (3) emergency response activities of workplace emergency response teams or emergency response activities already covered under specified OSHA standards (29 CFR 1910.120, 1910.146, 1910.156, part 1915 subpart P, 1926.65, and 1926.1211); (4) work in indoor areas or vehicles where air conditioning consistently keeps ambient temperature below 80°F; (5) telework; and (6) sedentary indoor work where tasks are limited to sitting, occasional standing/walking, and occasional lifting of objects under ten pounds. OSHA treats employees exclusively performing these activities as out of scope. (Printed page 70811)

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating employees meeting the short-duration (<15 minutes) exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate employees exposed above the initial trigger for fifteen minutes or less in any sixty-minute period, OSHA relied on ORS and OEWS occupation-level data and specific rules for indoor and outdoor settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For indoor settings OSHA used ORS percentages of employees 'not exposed' and 'seldomly exposed' to extreme heat as reflective of the short-duration exemption; for outdoor settings OSHA used percentages of employees that either 'do not work outdoors' or 'seldomly work outdoors.' OSHA multiplied these percentages by OEWS industry occupation employment shares and aggregated to 4-digit NAICS; for industries missing in OEWS, OSHA used 2-digit NAICS averages. (Printed page 70811)

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation for feedback on data sources and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA explicitly requests feedback on alternative data sources, estimation methods, and assumptions used to estimate numbers of firms, establishments, employment, and receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA identifies specific areas where it filled data gaps (e.g., agriculture, local/state government, rail/postal) and asks for comments and alternative approaches, indicating that some methodological choices (like one establishment = one firm) are provisional and open to stakeholder input. (Printed page 70809)
